body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Dragon variation
]

 6...Bg7 

7. f3 is the main move. This controls the g4-square and so denies Black ...Ng4, therefore allows White to play Qd2 next and castle long (the Bb5+ idea, which refuted 6...Ng4??, is less powerful now that Black's king can access f8). The pawn on f3 also supports the e4 pawn, liberating the knight from that duty, and can support a king-side pawn storm (g4, h4, g5, h5). 

7. Be2 transposes to the classical variation. This allows White to castle short instead, 7...O-O 8. O-O Nc6, with the idea of playing f4 and perhaps e5 (9. Nb3 Be6 10. f4 Qc8 is the Tartakower line), or attacking down the centre with Qd2 and Rad1 (9. Qd2 Bd7 10. Rad1, the battery variation). This sideline is much quieter but has been employed by many players.

7. Qd2!? immediately allows 7...Ng4 8. Bg5 h6 9. Bh4 Nc6, and it is more awkward for White to launch an attack. 

7. Bc4 almost always transposes into the old main line following 7...O-O 8. f3 Nc6 9. Qd2.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Yugoslav attack
]

 7. f3 · Yugoslav attack 
White's f-pawn defends e4, freeing the c3-knight from the duty, and controls the g4-square. This prevents ...Ng4, which Black was threatening to play and game time on White's bishop. The pawn on f3 is critical for supporting a king's side attack with g4, h4, and h5 in the future, where White aims to take advantage of the "hook" in the Black king's side, the g6 pawn. 

7...O-O is the main move, which gets the king to safety, and aims to setup a sharp and exciting game involving opposite-sides castling. 

7...Nc6 is the Belezky line. Usually this is just a small move order difference, and transposes to the main line after 8. Qd2 O-O. However, seeing that White is already preparing to storm the king's side, Black's idea may be to avoid castling completely. 

7...a6!? is an alternative. The move ...a6 on turn five is the start of the Najdorf variation, so this line that mixes the Najdorf with the dragon is given the twee name dragondorf. That's where the similarities end, though: the usual way of combatting the English attack (the Yugoslav's cousin in the Najdorf) involves ...e5 and ...Be6, where ...a6 serves to prevent Nb5 or Bb5+, but a pawn on e5 is hardly desirable in the Dragon with Black's bishop on g7. Instead the idea of ...a6 in the dragondorf is usually to support ...b5, and Black plays with a queen's side fianchetto and avoids castling.

[Diagram:
- FEN: 1rnbq1rk/1pp2ppb/p3p1np/8/4NP2/3N1BP1/1PPP3P/PR2QKB1
- Name: Yugoslav Attack
]

The Yugoslav Attack continues with 7...O-O. In the Yugoslav, Black castles kingside while White castles queenside, leading to an opposite-side-castling game where speed is important. Black often pushes on the queenside with a5 and b5 and continues advancing those pawns, while White plays g4 and h4 and continues advancing those pawns. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 is a key piece in Black's attack on the queenside and what makes the Dragon the Dragon.

White's most popular continuation is 8. Qd2, preparing for a queenside castle.

Second is 8. Bc4, which often transposes to the main line.

 7. Ng4?? 

Black attacks White's bishop, but falls into a common amateur trap.It is the fourth move in the Lichess database, played over 24,000 times as of May 2026.

White's queen attack's Black's knight, but it is currently guarded by their light square bishop. 7. Bb5+ cuts off that protection. 

If Black blocks the check with 7...Nd7, their bishop no longer guards g4. If 7...Bd7, the bishop becomes pinned and so also does not guard g4. 

If 7...Nc6, White can trade knights, 8. Nxc6 (attacking the queen) bxc6, and 9. Bxc6+ forks the king and rook.

[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Dragon Variation, Levenfish Variation | ECO Code: B71]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...d6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 > 4...Nf6 > 5. Nc3 > 5...g6 > 6. f4 (Sicilian Defense: Dragon Variation, Levenfish Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 g6 6. f4]
body:
Levenfish Variation 

[Diagram:
- FEN: 1rnbqkb1/rpp2pp1/p3p1np/8/4NPP1/3N4/1PPP3P/PR1BQKB1
- Name: Sicilian Defence, Dragon, Levenfish Variation
]

This move has a few ideas connoted to it. The primary idea is to push e5, since this pawn idea gains central influence and is now prepared by f4. White can also look to put the knight back onto f3 and play the position like a Grand Prix attack, with future ideas of swinging the white queen onto the kingside through the e1-h4 diagonal. Against some sidelines, white can also consider castling long!

 The point - 6...Bg7?! 7. e5! 
The natural looking 6...Bg7 is actually theoretically inaccurate. This runs into White's primary idea of the Levenfish, to push e5. White does this immediately with 7. e5 and then can claim a slight, nagging edge in the upcoming variations because of the advanced e-pawn.

White should seek active play with Bb5+ and Qe2 to support the pawn before deciding which way to castle, both leading to viable positions

 Main Line - 6...Nc6 
The best move since it immediately covers the threat of e5. This idea effectively killed the Levenfish variation pre-2000. Black develops the queenside knight. Here, White has traditionally gone for the line 7. Nxc6!? bxc6 8. e5 which is somewhat favourable for black upon 8...Nd7! 9. exd6 exd6 leading to an interesting pawn structure. A sounder alternative several high profile games have included is the idea of 7. Nf3!? swinging the knight back to the kingside and looking to play a slower game on the kingside.

 Other sidelines 
6...Nbd7 is traditionally met by 7. Nf3, although in recent times engines have preferred queen developments such as 7. Qe2, the choice of Grandmaster Gevorg Harutjunyan.

6...a6 aims to stop a piece landing on b5 and constructs a sort of Dragondorf setup. Here White can choose between 7. e5 and 7. Nf3.

 Statistics 
351 games in Lichess Masters database.

White wins 32 percent of games. 29 percent are drawn. 38% have black emerge victorious.

### Continuations & Sub-variations:
- **6...Bg7**: [Diagram:
- FEN: 2rnbqk1/1r1pp2p/pbp4p/1np5/8/1NPP4/1N6/PPP3PP
]

Black fell for the trap of 7. e5!. (FEN: `2rnbqk1/1r1pp2p/pbp4p/1np5/8/1NPP4/1N6/PPP3PP`)

[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Chekhover Variation | ECO Code: B53]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...d6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Qxd4 (Sicilian Defense: Chekhover Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Qxd4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Chekhover variation
]

 4. Qxd4 · Chekhover variation 

White recaptures on d4 with their queen. This is an irregular continuation that avoids the main line Open Sicilians.  

Usually it is considered unprincipled to develop one's queen early because it can be a target affording the enemy valuable tempo. However, here White argues that their queen is hard for Black to exploit because they have played ...d6. 

After 4...Nc6, attacking the queen, White pins and trades off the knight with 5. Bb5 Bd7 6. Bxc6. Then, the usual continuation is 6...Bxc6 7. Nc3 Nf6 8. Bg5 e6 9. O-O-O Be7 10. Rhe1 O-O. 

4...a6 prepares ...Nc6 to gain time on the queen by cutting out the response Bb5. One line is 5. c4 Nc6 6. Qd2; another line is to trade the queens off with 5. Be3 Nc6 6. Qb6 Qxb6 7. Bxb6. 

 History 

The earliest recorded appearance of this opening was in the third unofficial chess Olympiad, in Munich in 1936.Uulberg v Kremer. Chessgames.com 

Vitaly Chekhover (1908―1965) was a Soviet chess player from St. Petersburg, who played this variation in 1938.Chekhover v Lisitsin, 1938. Chessgames.com

[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Modern Variations, Tartakower | ECO Code: B50]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...d6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. c3 (Sicilian Defense: Modern Variations, Tartakower)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. c3]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Tartakower gambit
]

 4. c3 · Tartakower gambit 
White offers a pawn for quicker development and open c- and d-files. 

If Black accepts, 4...dxc3, then this is much like the Smith-Morra gambit (2. d4 cxd4 3. c3). Since they have already committed a pawn to ...d6, Black must play a line against the Smith-Morra involving ...d6 (e.g. the classical or Scheveningen formation defences). In this way White has move-ordered Black out of the more common Smith-Morra lines. 

If Black doesn't want to allow White to chose which Smith-Morra line they are to play, they can instead decline the gambit with 4...Nf6. A continuation is 5. e5 dxe5 6. Nxe5 Nbd7 7. Qxd4 e6 8. Bb5 a6 9. Nxd7 Bxd7 10. Bxd7+ Qxd7 11. Qxd7+ Nxd7.

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e5
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Jalalabad Variation | ECO Code: B27]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e5 (Sicilian Defense: Jalalabad Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e5]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Jalalabad variation
]

 2...e5? · Jalalabad variation 

Sorry, but JalalaVeryBad.―Anish Giri

In the Jalalabad variation, Black responds to e4 with both e5 and c5 (in either the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 c5? or 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e5?). This gives up Black's central e-pawn. This is not considered sound. 

After 3. Nxe5, Black can play 3...Nc6, offering to trade knights and take the game in a Stafford gambit-style direction, or 3...Qe7 looking to recover the pawn. 

3...Nc6 offers to trade knights. 4. Nxc6 dxc6 and the position resembles a Stafford gambit where Black is down a tempo, having played c5 instead of Nf6. There is no immediately threat to e4 and the position is a lot less precarious for White. 

3...Qe7 and Black looks to recover the pawn after 4. Nf3 Qxe4+ 5. Be2. Unfortunately White can hold onto the pawn with 4. d4 cxd4 5. Qxd4 (protecting knight and e pawn) Nc6 6. Nxc6 dxc6 +-. 

3...d6?! to kick the knight seems very weakening while Black's king is still in the centre. 

 History 

Sam Sloan explains he invented the opening while incarcerated for six weeks in Jalalabad prison in Afghanistan. He played it in a Marshall Chess Club tournament in 1978, where he defeated Jans Pamiljens with the 3...Qe7 continuation in a game that was published in Chess Life. Writing around 2002, Sloan recalled he had played it at other times in the late 70s, but that he thought his ex-wife had taken his score sheets. Of the opening, he said, "I still think that the Jalalabad Defense is playable."  

It received some online revival as an unorthodox gambit line online in 2020.

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: French Variation | ECO Code: B40]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 (Sicilian Defense: French Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6]
body:
2...e6 · French Sicilian 
Black opens up the a3-f8 diagonal for their dark squared bishop, while also controlling the d5 square for a second time. This prepares to play ...d5 and recapture with a pawn, gaining further central control. 

 Open the centre 

3. d4 is the main move. This is the standard open Sicilian plan: 3...cxd4 4. Nxd4. The centre is open and both of White's bishops are ready to come into the game. Then Black has a choice of how to proceed: the main French Sicilians are the Kan, Paulsen, Taimanov, or four knights variations. 

3. Nc3 is also possible. This postpones d4 while White waits for more information on which Sicilian Black will choose.  

 Anti-Sicilians 

There is also a variety of "anti-Sicilians" (Sicilians that aren't the open Sicilian) available to White, avoiding the main line and aiming to exploit the fact that 2...e6 blocked Black's c8 bishop. Against 2...d6 or 2...Nc6, the main anti-Sicilian is 3. Bb5, but it is not so effective here following 2...e6. If White still wishes to avoid the open Sicilian, they might opt for one of the following instead. 

3. c3 is the delayed Alapin Sicilian. The idea is to support playing d4 and keep the pawn there. While similar in character to the Alapin played on turn two (1. e4 c5 2. c3), playing c3 on the third move, after Black has committed a pawn to 2...e6, means Black has different options for how to proceed.

3. c4 is the Kramnik Sicilian, creating a "Maroczy bind" position where White contests the d5 square. 

3. b3 is the Westerinen attack, preparing to fianchetto the bishop. 

3. d3 may lead to a king's Indian-type position. White recognises that the position is a bit like a French defence (1. e4 e6), just where Black has already played ...c5 and hasn't gotten to ...d5 yet. White may start with 3. Qe2 or 3. g3 and reach the same set-up. 

 History 

Carl Jaenisch (1813―1872) may have been the first one to give this the name "French". In his 19th century treatise on chess, he grouped together 1...c5 followed by 2...e6 (2...e6 was the main variation at the time) with 1...e6 as the "French Openings", writing, "Far from being 'irregular,' they afford a line of defence more secure than [1...e5], but the Kings being severally less exposed, the game becomes much more tedious." (translation of )

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Westerinen Attack
]

 3. b3 
This opening has some very interesting ideas. With this move White prepares to fianchetto the dark squared bishop to b2 but depending on what Black plays next White's ideas aren't really clear.

Black can continue with the usual Taimanov or Kan setup and Black can also play the /4...d5/ pawn break, but the most played move in the chess database right now is /4...b6/.

 3. b3 
This opening has some very interesting ideas. With this move White prepares to fianchetto the dark squared bishop to b2 but depending on what Black plays next White's ideas aren't really clear.

Black can continue with the usual Taimanov or Kan setup and Black can also play the /4...d5/ pawn break, but the most played move in the chess database right now is /4...b6/.

[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Open Sicilian with 2...e6
]

 3. d4 · Open Sicilian with 2...e6 

White plays 3. d4, inviting Black to trade a pawn and open the position. 

3...cxd4 is the main move. Black captures towards the centre with a flank pawn, breaking up White's two pawn centre. Once White recaptures 4. Nxd4, Black has two central pawns to White's one, and a semi-open c-file to use. White meanwhile has opened attacking lines: both bishops have access to the game, and their queen has the semi-open d-file. After the trade of pawns is complete, Black then has a choice of ...e6 Sicilians, the most popular of which are the Kan (4...a6), Taimanov (4...Nc6), four knights (both ...Nc6 and ...Nf6), or Kveinis (4...Qb6) variations. 

Very minor sidelines include:

 3...d5!?, the Marshall counterattack.
 3...a6!?, the Drazic variation.

[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 (Sicilian Defense: French Variation, Open)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Open Sicilian with ...e6
]

 3...cxd4 
Black captures White's d-pawn with cxd4 to reduce White's control of the centre. They are now playing with two centre pawns to White's one. 

4. Nxd4 recaptures the pawn. The knight may subsequently move to b3 to assist in the defence of their king following queenside castling. A knight on d4 also eyes the f5 square and once the king is safe on the queenside can support the advance of a barrage of pawns at Black's castled position.

Also in keeping with the position is the gambit 4. c3, the Smith-Morra gambit deferred. After 4...dxc3 5. Nxc3 Nc6 the usual Smith-Morra main line is reached. In return for the pawn, White obtains a lead in development and aims to fully open the c-file to counter Black's influence thereof.

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation | ECO Code: B44]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 > 4...Nc6 (Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6]
body:
4...Nc6 · Taimanov variation 
4...Nc6 in the e6 Sicilian is the Taimanov, named for Russian GM Mark Taimanov who popularised the opening in the 1960s. 

While Nc6 doesn't make a threat on e4, 5. Nc3 is White's usual response all the same. After, Black's principal options are 5...Nf6, the Four Knights Sicilian, or 5...Qc7, the Bastrikov variation. 

With 5...Qc7, Black wants to focus on their queenside development first: a6, b5, Bb7 and Rc8, with the dark-square bishop developing to e7 or b4. White's plans include the English Attack (with Nc3, Be3, Qd2 and O-O-O), or Nc3, Be2 and O-O. 

5. Nb5 is the chief sideline, where White moves to exploit the hole Black left on d6 when they played 2...e6. White has two attackers on d6 and Black only one defender, the bishop, so 5...a6? allows 6. Nd6+ Bxd6 7. Qxd6 ∓. Black gets the bishop pair and their Queen is all up in White's business. The only way for White to add a defender to d6 is 5...d6 (now the queen sees d6), after which 6. c4 or 6.Bf4 usually follow. 

5. Nxc6?!, exchanging the knights, is a sideline only really seen at the amateur level. Unlike in the Four Knights Sicilian, where exchanging the knights lets White push e5 with tempo, it is of no real benefit to White here. After 5...bxc6, Black can easily play 6...d5 with extra support from the c pawn. 6. e5? is met with 6...Qa5+ forking the pawn. 

5. c4 is a Maróczy bind- or Kramnik-style line where White looks to gain space. 5...Nf6 6. Nc3 Bb4 equalises.

 History 

The Taimanov Sicilian evolved out of the older Paulsen variation of the Sicilian (a Sicilian with with e6, a6, and Qc7). Curiously, in his book, Taimanov himself didn't consider 4...Nc6 to be the defining moving of his system, which he describes as just one of a number of possible move orders of the Paulsen. Rather, he considered the defining move of the Taimanov to be delaying Qc7 in favour of Nge7, describing "Black's basic opening plan in... the Taimanov system [is to remove] active White pieces from the d4 outpost... by an exchange of the knight in the centre [Nxd4 Qxd4] and the subsequent 'tempo' transfer of the 'knight understudy' to c6."

header:

[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 > 4...Nc6 > 5. Nb5 (Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation, Szén Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5]
body:
5. Nb5 · Szén variation 

With 5. Nb5 White moves to exploit Black's dark square weaknesses. When Black played 2...e6, they left a hole on the d6 square. 

White has two attackers on d6 and Black only one defender, the bishop, so 5...a6? allows 6. Nd6+ Bxd6 7. Qxd6 ∓. White gets the bishop pair and their Queen is all up in Black's business. 

5...d6 is the only way for Black to add a defender, allowing the black queen to see d6. White can then follow with 6. c4 or 6. Bf4. White will have to spend some tempo retreating their knight to somewhere safer, before or after it is kicked by a6. White chooses either knights on a3 and c3, or c3 and d2. 

5...d5? technically adds a defender to d6, but after 6. exd5 exd5 7. Bf4 takes control of the square again. (7. Qxd5 also works: 7...Qxd5? Nc7+ recovers the queen.) 

5...Nf6 is an alternative: Black postpones White playing Nd6 by threatening their e4 pawn. After 6. Nc3 to defend it, Black can then choose to play 7...d6 after all, or 7...Bb4, pinning the knight, instead, then 7. a3 Bxc3+ 8. Nxc3 d5.

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation, Szén Variation | ECO Code: B44]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 > 4...Nc6 > 5. Nb5 > 5...d6 (Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation, Szén Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6]
body:
5...d6 

Black prevents White's knight coming in to d6. 

White can then follow with 6. c4 or 6. Bf4. 

6. Bf4 acts to provoke 6...e5, weakening the d5 square and leading the game into a Kalashnikov-style Sicilian, with Black's pawns on e5 and d6. After 6...e5 the bishop falls back to 7. Be3. Then Black typically looks to kick White's misplaced knight, 7...a6, or develop while attacking White's e4 pawn, 7...Nf6.

6. c4 is more common: White sets up the Maroczy bind structure to control d5. Black can play 6...a6 to kick White's knight, or 6...Nf6 followed by 7...a6: the idea being to first induce N1c3, then White's other knight has no choice but to retreat to the passive a3 square when kicked. White will have moved the same knight four times in the opening: in exchange they hope that their pawns on e4 and c4 will restrict Black's space and so make their development harder.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Szén variation
]

 6. c4 

White sets up the Maroczy bind structure to control d5. Between their c and e pawns, and having induced Black to play d6 and restrict their own dark square bishop, they hope to keep Black's position cramped, hampering their development, and that this will make up for the loss of tempo White incurred in moving their knight multiple times in the opening. 

If 6...a6 straight away, Black kicks White's knight and they are forced to move it again: usually to c3. 

Black usually plays 6...Nf6 first, threatening Nxe4 with the idea of inducing 7. N1c3, followed by 7...a6 to kick the knight to 8. Na3 where it is on the rim and therefore grim, but from where it overprotect the c4 pawn and doesn't obstruct the White queen's support of d5.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Szén variation
]

 7...a6 

7...a6 kicks White's knight. 

Its available squares are d4 or a3. 

The most common move is 8. Na3. This places a knight on the rim, but at least it overdefends c4 in case Black hopes to make use of the half-open file and play ...Rc8 one day. 

8. Nd4 reduces White's control of d5, and allows Black to untangle with 8...d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nxd5 11. Nxc6 bxc6 (see diagram). The position is equal but now open, and White is no longer able to keep Black suffocating in their side of the board as they had hoped.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Szén variation
]

 8. Na3 

White saves their knight with 8. Na3. 

The position is looking cramped for Black. Those pawns on c4 and e4 prevent them from playing d5 and gaining more space. Meanwhile, Black's pawns on d6 and e6 prevent Black from developing their bishops very actively. 

They have three typical continuations. 

Black still has their bishops to develop, so option one is to develop their light-square bishop, in which case first Black must play 8...b6 to make room to fianchetto it.

Option two is to develop their dark-square bishop. Fianchettoing it is inconceivable of course because of how weak f6 will become. Since White induced them to play 5...d6, there is only one place left for it, so Black may as well play 8...Be7 and get it over with, then at least they can castle. 

Option three is to discard both these options as too timid, throw caution at the wind, and kick open the Maroczy bind with 8...d5 anyway. This is an especially good continuation if it is 1985 and you are Garry Kasparov, after whom the audacious play, the Garry gambit, is named.

[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation, Gary Gambit | ECO Code: B44]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 > 4...Nc6 > 5. Nb5 > 5...d6 > 6. c4 > 6...Nf6 > 7. N1c3 > 7...a6 > 8. Na3 > 8...d5 (Sicilian Defense: Taimanov Variation, Gary Gambit)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Garry gambit
]

 8...d5!? · Garry gambit 

Black challenges White in the centre to open up the position. 

White has four attackers to Black's three defenders. However, after 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5, Black intends to play 10...Nb4, bringing another attacker. 

 History 
The Garry gambit was first played by Garry Kasparov in two games of the 1985 World Championship match with Anatoly Karpov (see sample game).

After the discovery of the continuation 12. Be3 Bxe3 13. Qa4+! (see below) this fell out of favour for Black.

 Sample game 
 Karpov v Kasparov, 1985 
The sixteenth game of the World Championship match.Karpov v Kasparov 1985 - Chessgames.com

1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5

Kasparov plays the "Garry gambit". 

[Diagram:
- Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nb4
- Name: Position after 10...Nb4.
]

9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nb4

This position had already been reached in their twelfth game of the match. In that game, Karpov (playing White) continued 11. Bc4, a natural move to defend the pawn, and continued cautiously before having to settle for a draw: 11...Bg4 (compelling White's bishop to retreat) 12. Be2 Bxe2 13. Qxe2+ Qe7 14. Be3 Nbxd5 (Black recovers the pawn) 15. Nc2 Nxe3 16. Nxe3 Qe6 17. O-O Bc5 18. Rfe1 O-O ½-½. 

11. Be2 

This time White intends to control d5 with a Be2-Bf3 manoeuvre. 

11...Bc5

Rather than take back the pawn, Black leaves it and focuses on development instead. They can quickly capitalise on good, active squares for their pieces, while White's knight on a3 is passive. 

Kasparov analysed 11...Nbxd5 12. O-O Be7 13. Nxd5 Nxd5 14. Bf3 (attacking knight) Be6 (defending knight) 15. Nc2! as better for White. The c2 knight threatens to come to d4, where it can take bishop on e6 that is tied down to protect the knight. Black therefore avoids taking the pawn because of the difficulty in defending the knight on the d5 square. 

12. O-O

When Karpov faced this line again in 1986, he played the improvement 12. Be3 Bxe3 13. Qa4+! forking the now-undefended knight on b4.Karpov v van der Wiel, 1986 - Chessgames.com

12...O-O 13. Bf3 Bf5

Black locks out the a3 knight from play. It now cannot go to c2, and Nc4 allows Bd3, forking the knight and the rook. (In fact, modern engines are happy with the transformation 14. Nc4 Bd3 15. Ne3 Bxf1 16. Kxf1 for White: willing to sacrifice the exchange to eliminate Black's active bishop and revive the prospects of White's knight). 

[Diagram:
- Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nb4 11. Be2 Bc5 12. O-O O-O 13. Bf3 Bf5 14. Bg5 Re8 15. Qd2 b5 16. Rad1 Nd3
- Name: Black's monstrous knight.
]

14. Bg5 Re8 15. Qd2 b5 16. Rad1 Nd3

Black's knight takes over a superb outpost and dominates White's position. Black threatens b3, forking the knights. 

17. Nab1 h6 18. Bh4 b4 19. Na4 Bd6 

White's position is close to paralysis: Black's monstrous knight is preventing White from bringing their rooks into the game, White's knights have been pushed to the rim with nowhere to go, and now Black threatens to trap White's queen with Rc8 and Bf4. 

20. Bg3 

Forced, to prevent White's queen becoming trapped. 

20...Rc8

Black had to discard two alternatives:

 20...Ne4 21. Bxe4 Bxe4, winning the bishop pair and weakening White's d5 pawn. Seirawan's analysis picks out the danger of 22. Qe3 as a continuation, allowing White to untangle their position by playing Qb6 to trade queens (though the engine likes this for Black. One continuation is 22...Bf5 23. Qb6 Bxg3 24. Qxd8 Bxh2+ 25. Kxh2 Raxd8). 
 20...Bxg3 21. hxg3 Qa5 22. b3 Rad8 23. Na3 (the b3 pawn is pinned to Black's queen) Nxd5 and Black wins the d5 pawn, then 24. Nc4 Qb5 25. Bxd5 Rxd5 26. Ne3 Rdd8 27. Nxf5 Qxf5. Kasparov believed he had more chance to play for advantage by avoiding the trades and "tightening the screws on the position [asking] White how he intends to solve his problems."

Black takes the open c-file and control of even more of White's space.

21. b3

To allow Nb2: White hopes to trade off Black's monstrous knight. 

21...g5 22. Bxd6 Qxd6 23. g3 Nd7 24. Bg2 Qf6

White can't get in Nb2 now. Their a4 knight is so out of play that they are practically down a piece; their b1 knight is no better.

25. a3 a5 26. axb4 axb4 27. Qa2

White is desperate to untangle their position and get some piece activity. Unable to shift Black's b pawn, White moves the queen to make room for Nd2 instead.

27...Bg6

Black can meet Nd2 with Re2!, pinning the knight to White's queen. However, if say 27...h5 28. Nd2 Re2, White has the defensive resource Bf2Modern engine analysis is actually is unimpressed by the Bf2 resource. The engine finds 27...h5 28. Nd2 Re2 29. Bf3 Rxf2!  taking the pawn instead of the knight, very good for Black: 30. Rxf2 Nxf2 31. Kxf2 Qd4+ 32. Kg2 and Black may have given up a knight but the threat of Rc2! is devastating.. By moving their bishop back, Black allows their queen to control f2 and 28. Nd2 Re2 29. Bf3 Rxd2 30. Qxd2 Qxf3 wins two pieces for a rook. 

28. d6 g4 29. Qd2 Kg7 30. f3 Qxd6 31. fxg4 Qd4+ 32. Kh1 Nf6 33. Rf4 Ne4 34. Qxd3 Nf2+ 35. Rxf2 Bxd3 36. Rfd2 Qe3 37. Rxd3 Rc1 38. Nb2 Qf2 39. Nd2 Rxd1+ 40. Nxd1 Re1+ 

Black has mate in 2 (41. Nf1 Rxf1+ 42. Bxf1 Qxf1#). White resigns.

Be3 Nbxd5 (Black recovers the pawn) 15. Nc2 Nxe3 16. Nxe3 Qe6 17. O-O Bc5 18. Rfe1 O-O ½-½. 

11. Be2 

This time White intends to control d5 with a Be2-Bf3 manoeuvre. 

11...Bc5

Rather than take back the pawn, Black leaves it and focuses on development instead. They can quickly capitalise on good, active squares for their pieces, while White's knight on a3 is passive. 

Kasparov analysed 11...Nbxd5 12. O-O Be7 13. Nxd5 Nxd5 14. Bf3 (attacking knight) Be6 (defending knight) 15. Nc2! as better for White. The c2 knight threatens to come to d4, where it can take bishop on e6 that is tied down to protect the knight. Black therefore avoids taking the pawn because of the difficulty in defending the knight on the d5 square. 

12. O-O

When Karpov faced this line again in 1986, he played the improvement 12. Be3 Bxe3 13. Qa4+! forking the now-undefended knight on b4.Karpov v van der Wiel, 1986 - Chessgames.com

12...O-O 13. Bf3 Bf5

Black locks out the a3 knight from play. It now cannot go to c2, and Nc4 allows Bd3, forking the knight and the rook. (In fact, modern engines are happy with the transformation 14. Nc4 Bd3 15. Ne3 Bxf1 16. Kxf1 for White: willing to sacrifice the exchange to eliminate Black's active bishop and revive the prospects of White's knight). 

[Diagram:
- Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nb4 11. Be2 Bc5 12. O-O O-O 13. Bf3 Bf5 14. Bg5 Re8 15. Qd2 b5 16. Rad1 Nd3
- Name: Black's monstrous knight.
]

14. Bg5 Re8 15. Qd2 b5 16. Rad1 Nd3

Black's knight takes over a superb outpost and dominates White's position. Black threatens b3, forking the knights. 

17. Nab1 h6 18. Bh4 b4 19. Na4 Bd6 

White's position is close to paralysis: Black's monstrous knight is preventing White from bringing their rooks into the game, White's knights have been pushed to the rim with nowhere to go, and now Black threatens to trap White's queen with Rc8 and Bf4. 

20. Bg3 

Forced, to prevent White's queen becoming trapped. 

20...Rc8

Black had to discard two alternatives:

 20...Ne4 21. Bxe4 Bxe4, winning the bishop pair and weakening White's d5 pawn. Seirawan's analysis picks out the danger of 22. Qe3 as a continuation, allowing White to untangle their position by playing Qb6 to trade queens (though the engine likes this for Black. One continuation is 22...Bf5 23. Qb6 Bxg3 24. Qxd8 Bxh2+ 25. Kxh2 Raxd8). 
 20...Bxg3 21. hxg3 Qa5 22. b3 Rad8 23. Na3 (the b3 pawn is pinned to Black's queen) Nxd5 and Black wins the d5 pawn, then 24. Nc4 Qb5 25. Bxd5 Rxd5 26. Ne3 Rdd8 27. Nxf5 Qxf5. Kasparov believed he had more chance to play for advantage by avoiding the trades and "tightening the screws on the position [asking] White how he intends to solve his problems."

Black takes the open c-file and control of even more of White's space.

21. b3

To allow Nb2: White hopes to trade off Black's monstrous knight. 

21...g5 22. Bxd6 Qxd6 23. g3 Nd7 24. Bg2 Qf6

White can't get in Nb2 now. Their a4 knight is so out of play that they are practically down a piece; their b1 knight is no better.

25. a3 a5 26. axb4 axb4 27. Qa2

White is desperate to untangle their position and get some piece activity. Unable to shift Black's b pawn, White moves the queen to make room for Nd2 instead.

27...Bg6

Black can meet Nd2 with Re2!, pinning the knight to White's queen. However, if say 27...h5 28. Nd2 Re2, White has the defensive resource Bf2Modern engine analysis is actually is unimpressed by the Bf2 resource. The engine finds 27...h5 28. Nd2 Re2 29. Bf3 Rxf2!  taking the pawn instead of the knight, very good for Black: 30. Rxf2 Nxf2 31. Kxf2 Qd4+ 32. Kg2 and Black may have given up a knight but the threat of Rc2! is devastating.. By moving their bishop back, Black allows their queen to control f2 and 28. Nd2 Re2 29. Bf3 Rxd2 30. Qxd2 Qxf3 wins two pieces for a rook. 

28. d6 g4 29. Qd2 Kg7 30. f3 Qxd6 31. fxg4 Qd4+ 32. Kh1 Nf6 33. Rf4 Ne4 34. Qxd3 Nf2+ 35. Rxf2 Bxd3 36. Rfd2 Qe3 37. Rxd3 Rc1 38. Nb2 Qf2 39. Nd2 Rxd1+ 40. Nxd1 Re1+ 

Black has mate in 2 (41. Nf1 Rxf1+ 42. Bxf1 Qxf1#). White resigns.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Bastrikov variation
]

 5...Qc7 · Bastrikov variation 
Black chooses to develop their queen to a safe square where it has good scope.

6. Be3 is the most common move. White develops their bishop to an active square where the knight on d4 is defended from any potential ...Nxd4 exchanges that may happen in the future. White may be preparing to castle long, 6...a6 7. Qd2 Nf6 8. O-O-O, or is overdefending their knight so that they may play 7. Bd3 and castle short.  

6. Be2 develops the king's bishop without obstructing the queen's defence of d4, and prepares to castle short, 6...a6 7. O-O. 

6. Nxc6 does not wait to exchange knights. White decides that it is finally time to settle the trade offer by accepting.

6. Ndb5 is the most aggressive move. White immediately goes on the offensive and attacks the newly placed queen on c7 with their knight.

[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...e6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 > 4...Qb6 (Sicilian Defense: Kveinis Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Qb6]
body:
4...Qb6 · Kveinis variation 

The rare and razor-sharp Kveinis (or Kveinys) variation has often been considered inferior to other variations of the French Sicilian, but statistics show it scores the best of any of Black's turn four moves at the club level, and respectably well at grandmaster level, too. It is especially efficacious as a surprise weapon in blitz and bullet games. 

...Qb6 pressures b2, White's knight on d4, and beyond it the weak f2 square. Much of the variation's club-level success comes from White underestimating ...Bc5, where Black stacks power against f2. For example, 5. c4? Bc5! and Black threatens to win the knight. 6. Be3 Nc6 (increases pressure on d4) 7. Nxc6? Bxe3 8. fxe3 Qxe3+ . 

5. Nc3 is the most common move in amateur databases, but leads to sharp positions where Black gets a strong attack. After 5...Bc5 6. Be3 Nc6, White must find 7. Na4, and the line continues 7...Qa5+ 8. c3 Bxd4 9. Bxd4 Nxd4 10. Qxd4 e5. Though the game is even by engine, Black has more practical success. (7. Nxc6?, as above, is a common mistake. Another trap is 7. Nb3?? Bxf2+ 8. Kd2 Qe3#.)

5. Nb2 is the main line. From here the knight is less of a target, and it controls c5 to deny Black ...Bc5. 

Many other lines are playable, including 5. Be3 Bc5 6. Na3! threatening Nc4. Generally Black finds the pawn on b2 is poisonous, though taking it often leads to sharp lines that may pose White practical difficulties. For instance, the most common line after 5. Be3 in the Lichess amateur database is 5...Qxb2?! 6. Nd2 Bb4?? 7. Rb1 Bxd2+ 8. Bxd2?? (needed was 8. Kxd2!) Qxd4 .

History

4...Qb6 was a pet line of Aloyzas Kveinys (lt) (1962―2018), a Lithuanian International Master.e.g. Klovans v Kveinys, 1986. Chessgames.com It has been employed by strong grandmasters including Nigel Shorte.g. Polgar v Short, 1997. Chessgames.com and Judit Polgar.e.g. Nunn v Polgar, 1992. Chessgames.com

Na4, and the line continues 7...Qa5+ 8. c3 Bxd4 9. Bxd4 Nxd4 10. Qxd4 e5. Though the game is even by engine, Black has more practical success. (7. Nxc6?, as above, is a common mistake. Another trap is 7. Nb3?? Bxf2+ 8. Kd2 Qe3#.)

5. Nb2 is the main line. From here the knight is less of a target, and it controls c5 to deny Black ...Bc5. 

Many other lines are playable, including 5. Be3 Bc5 6. Na3! threatening Nc4. Generally Black finds the pawn on b2 is poisonous, though taking it often leads to sharp lines that may pose White practical difficulties. For instance, the most common line after 5. Be3 in the Lichess amateur database is 5...Qxb2?! 6. Nd2 Bb4?? 7. Rb1 Bxd2+ 8. Bxd2?? (needed was 8. Kxd2!) Qxd4 .

History

4...Qb6 was a pet line of Aloyzas Kveinys (lt) (1962―2018), a Lithuanian International Master.e.g. Klovans v Kveinys, 1986. Chessgames.com It has been employed by strong grandmasters including Nigel Shorte.g. Polgar v Short, 1997. Chessgames.com and Judit Polgar.e.g. Nunn v Polgar, 1992. Chessgames.com

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...f5
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Brussels Gambit | ECO Code: B27]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...f5 (Sicilian Defense: Brussels Gambit)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 f5]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Brussels gambit
]

 2...f5? · Brussels gambit 

Black offers the f-pawn, hoping to deflect White's e-pawn from control of d5. However, it comes with severe trade-offs. Moving the f-pawn opens the a2-g8 and e8-h5 diagonals, and if White accepts the pawn Black may find their unable to play ...d5 anyway, due to the weaknesses of the e6 and e5 squares. Therefore the gambit is not considered sound. 

After 3. exf5, Black may hope for compensation in the form of reducing White's control of the centre. In particular, Black can now play 3...d5. This may look appealing because it takes space in the centre and prepares to develop the bishop and recapture the pawn. However, playing ...d5 turns the e5 and e6 squares into  holes that White can exploit to pressure Black's position. For example, 4. Bb5+ Nc6 (4...Bd7 is better) 5. Ne5!: the knight jumps into the centre with the threat to take twice on c6 and win another pawn, and if 5...Bd7? 6. Qh5+! exploits the weakened king's side. 6...g6 7. fxg6 Nf6 8. g7+! Nxh5 9. gxh8=Q . 

Black may think it's wise to start with 3. Nf6 to control h5. After White plays 4. d4 cxd4 5. Nxd4, opening the position and readying their attack, Black may still not play 5...d5 due to 6. Bb5+ Bd7 7. Ne6!. 

3...Nh6?! has (for whatever reason) acquired the name the "double Dutch gambit". Black intends to recapture the pawn with the knight instead. White should of course allow it and focus on their development. 

 History 

Schiller includes this gambit in his 1998 book. He gives the line 3. exf5 d6 4. Bb5+ Bd7 5. Nd4!! (Schiller's annotation; Stockfish gives it ??)  cxd4 6. Qh5+ g6 7. fxg6 Nf6 8. g7+ Nxh5 9. gxh8=Q Bxb5 (?? per engine. Schiller misses 9. Nf6 and White's queen is stuck) 10. Qxh7 Nf4 11. d3 Nxg2+ 12. Kf1 Bc6 13. Qh5+ Kd7 14. Rg1 e5.

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon | ECO Code: B27]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...g6 (Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 g6]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Hyperaccelerated Dragon
]

 2...g6 · Hyperaccelerated Dragon 
Black prepares to fianchetto their king's bishop, ...Bg7. This is the start of the Hyperaccelerated Dragon. 

In the Accelerated Dragon, Black usually plays 2...Nc6 before preparing to fianchetto their bishop. This allows White the option of 3. Bb5, the Rossolimo attack. With the move order 2...g6, Black hopes to sidestep that line. 

The main continuation is the usual Open Sicilian plan: 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4, and 4...Nc6 transposes to the Accelerated Dragon, Rossolimo successfully avoided. White can continue with 5. Nc3, the conventional Open Sicilian move, or 5. c4, the tricky Maróczy bind, which clamps down on the d5 square with both e- and c-pawns. 

However, the 2...g6 move order gives White some other options that steer the game away from transposing into an Accelerated dragon, which Black must be prepared for:

 3. d4 cxd4 4. Qxd4!?, attacking Black's rook. The main continuation is 4...Nf6 5. e5 Nc6 6. Qa4 Nd5 7. Qe4.
 3. c3, a sort of deferred Alapin, is also strong.

3. c4 transposes to the Maróczy bind line after 3...Nc6 4. d4 cxd4 5. Nxd4 Bg7.

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon | ECO Code: B27]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...g6 > 3. c4 (Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 g6 3. c4]
body:
Sicilian - Hyper-Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind 

The Maróczy Bind Variation of the Hyper-Accelerated Dragon is a variation where white advances the c4 before playing Nc3, this also helps controlling the d5 square, after black fianchettos the bishop on g7, white will play Nc3 and d4, build a big and stable center, Similar to the Staunton-Cochrane Sicilian where white play e4, c4, and aims for d4.

 Possible moves for black 
After the move c4, black can decide on many moves but the most popular ones include:

3... Bg7

Possibly the most common one, the whole idea of the move g6 is to play fianchetto the bishop in the g7 square, after that move, white has mainly two great options, d4, immediately striking at the center, or, a slower move, which is Nc3, white can alternatively play the move d3, guarding both pawns, but the pawn on d3 will be an weakness for white as well as giving play time to develop both knights and then play d6, which wont be a weakness since they didn't commit the e-pawn forward.

3... Nc6

This is a possible transportion to the accelerated dragon, since after 4. d4 cxd4 5. Nxd4 and Bg7, the position is the same as if had committed the c-pawn after the move Nc6 instead of Bg7,white can choose not to transpose with the move Nc3, but the position will not be as great, according to modern-day engines like Stockfish.

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...g6/3. d4
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon | ECO Code: B27]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...g6 > 3. d4 (Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 g6 3. d4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Hyperaccelerated Dragon
]

 3. d4 
White plays 3. d4, the classic Open Sicilian move, to open up the centre while opening lines for their bishop and queen to develop. White is playing to maximise their activity. 

This gives White pawns on both d4 and e4 controlling great tracts in the middle of the board, so the main move is 3...cxd4 to break up White's powerful two-pawn centre, and after White recaptures, Black will have a central pawn majority and use of the half-open c-file. White can then retake the pawn with either 4. Nxd4, the conventional Open Sicilian move, or 4. Qxd4, which is an effective sideline against the Hyperaccelerated Dragon. 

3...Bg7!? is a sideline for Black, which transposes into the Pterodactyl defence (usually reached by an early ...c5 in the Modern defence). 4. dxc5 Qa4+ lets Black recover the pawn.

[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...g6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 (Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 g6 3. d4 cxd4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Hyperaccelerated dragon
]

 3...cxd4 

Black takes the d-pawn. This was the idea behind 1...c5: White can retake and Black has a central pawn majority (both d- and e-pawns). In exchange, White gets open lines for development. 

There are two ways to retake the pawn. 

4. Nxd4 is natural. 4...Nc6 transposes into the accelerated dragon Sicilian and Black has successfully avoided facing the Rossolimo variation through the hyperaccelerated move order. 

From there, the main continuations Black faces are 5. c4 or 5. Nc3. 4...Bg7 5. c4 Nc3 transposes. 4...Nf6 first, attacking e4, encourages 5. Nc3 so as to avoid facing 5. c4, though White can always play 5. f3 to keep the option of c4. 4...Nf6 5. e5? loses the pawn to 5...Qa5+. 

4. Qxd5 is an alternative that avoids a straight transposition into the accelerated dragon. This attacks h8, since Black has moved their g-pawn (4...Nc3?? 5. Qxh8! or 4...Bg7 5. Qxg7!). 

4...Nf6 and White has the tricky line 5. e5!? Nc6 6. Qa4 Nd5 7. Qe4 Ndb4?! 8. Bb5 Qa5?! 9. Nc3 (diagram), where e.g. 9...d5 10. exd6 Bf5 11. Qe5 f6 12. Bxc6+ Nxc6 13. Qxa5 Nxa5 14. dxe7 Bxe7 15. Nd4 Bb4.

[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon | ECO Code: B27]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. Nf3 > 2...g6 > 3. d4 > 3...cxd4 > 4. Nxd4 (Sicilian Defense: Hyperaccelerated Dragon)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 g6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Hyperaccelerated dragon
]

 4. Nxd4 
White recaptures according to the standard open Sicilian plan. 

Black can now transpose into the accelerated dragon with 4...Nc6. This is the main idea behind this move order: to reach the accelerated dragon while avoiding facing the Rossolimo sideline. White may play with 5. Nc3 or 5. c4, the Maróczy bind. 

4...Nf6 attacks the e4 pawn so encourages 5. Nc3, though White may play 5. f3 to keep the option of c4. 5. e5? loses the pawn to 5...Qa5+. After 5. Nc3, ...Qa5 does not come with check, so White is then threatening e5 (5...Nc6? 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. e5). Therefore Black usually answers 5. Nc3 with 5...d6, accepting they will not be playing ...d5 in one tempo and transposing into the regular dragon Sicilian. 

4...Bg7 typically transposes to the accelerated dragon by a slightly different move order. 5. c4 Nf6 6. Nc3 O-O 7. Be3 Nc6.

Mengarini Variation
Black can accept the gambit with 3...cxb4 but the best move is the drawish 3...Nf6, to which the best response is 4. b5.

3...cxb4 used to be the main line and is still often seen at amateur levels. The most common continuation is

4. axb4 Nxb4
5. d4 d5
6. c3 Nc6
7. exd5 Qxd5
8. Na3!

Now, Black needs to be precise: The natural moves 8...Nf6, 8...e5, and 8...e6 blunder 9. Nb5.

[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. b3]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Czerniak attack
]

 2. b3!? · Czerniak attack 
A rare but interesting sideline against the Sicilian, 2. b3 prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop to b2, where it will pressure Black's king's side. White usually intends to postpone opening the position, and has ideas of attacking on the kingside with f4, O-O, etc. 

The main continuation is 2...Nc6, although many "standard" Sicilian moves, 2...d6, 2...e6 are possible. 

2...b6, the queen's fianchetto variation, is challenging alternative where Black hopes to generate initiative by pressuring White's undefended e4 pawn.Morozevich v Polgar, 2014. Chessgames.com 

 History 
The earliest recorded appearance of 2. b3 was played by John Cochrane against Howard Staunton in 1843.Cochrane v Staunton, 1843. Chessgames.com 

Moshe Czerniak (1910―1984) was a Polish-Israeli International Master who specialised in this line.e.g. Czerniak v Benko, 1969. Chessgames.com

It also sometimes known as the Snyder variation after disgraced former chess coach Robert Michael Snyder, who published a book of analysis on the line in 1983, naming it after himself.

In modern times the line is associated with Grandmaster Alexander Morozevich (1977―), who played it exclusively against 1...c5 in the 2014 World Rapid and Blitz championships.World Blitz Championship (2014) (games of Alexander Morozevich). Chessgames.comWorld Rapid Championship (2014) (games of Alexander Morozevich). Chessgames.com

[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. b4]
body:
__NOTOC__

[Diagram:
- FEN: 2rnbqkb/nr1pp1pp/ppp5/7p/7P/2P5/8/P1PP1PPP
]

Sicilian Wing Gambit

2. b4 marks the Sicilian Wing Gambit. There are other wing gambits like this using the b-pawn (for instance, the Evans Gambit); however, this wing gambit is the most common one. The b-pawn push tries to undermine Black's c-pawn control of d4.

This gambit is unsound at the top level, and Black can safely accept it. However, it is common in amateur play.

Black's responses

2...cxb4. Black usually accepts the gambit. White is most likely to play 3. a3 to try to develop the knight by either recapturing on a3 or going to c3.

2...d5. Black can always decline the gambit and attack White's e-pawn.

]

 2...cxb4 · Wing Gambit Accepted 

Black bravely accepts the gambit. Since the gambit is of questionable soundness, it is best to accept it. 

One trap: a3 d5! (Countering in the center) exd5 Qxd5 axb4?? (White, in his eagerness to regain the pawn, forgot a simple tactic), Qe5+ wins the rook on a1. 

The recommended refutation is to counterattack in the center at the right time.

White's responses

3. a3.

3. d4.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Alapin variation
]

 2. c3 · Alapin variation 
This is one of the main "anti-Sicilians", a way for White to avoid the theory-dense open lines following 2. Nf3. 

2. c3 supports pushing the pawn to d4. If 2...Nc6!?, which is a common amateur try, 3. d4 cxd4 4. cxd4 and White has achieved a two-pawn centre. When they played 1...c5, Black had hoped for an edge by taking central pawn with a less-important flanking c-pawn, but this disappeared when White was able to recapture with their own flank pawn. The line continues 4...d5 5. exd5 (5. e5?! allows Black to play ...Bf5 and ...e6, for an improved French defence structure) Qxd5 6. Nf3 e5 7. Nc3 Bb4 8. Bd2 Bxc3 9. Bxc3 e4 10. Ne5 Nxe5 11. dxe5 Ne7

However, 2. c3 has the drawback of taking away the c3 square which White would otherwise like to place their knight. Black's two main moves, 2...d5 and 2...Nf6, seek to take advantage of this.

2...d5 threatens 3...dxe4, and after 3. exd5 Qxd5, the Barmen defence, White can still play 4. d4, but they no longer get two pawns in the centre and Black has a development lead. White is unable to play Nc3 with tempo on the queen because they have already occupied that square with a pawn, and Black is in no hurry to play ...cxd4 cxd4 and free the c3 square for White. 2...d5 is the old main line.

2...Nf6 has gained popularity and is now main response. 2...Nf6 attacks the pawn on e4, and White cannot defend with Nc3. The main line is 3. e5 Nd5 (3...Ne4? 4. d3! traps the knight) 4. d4 (threatening 5. c4 & 6. d5) cxd4, transposing into a Smith-Morra gambit declined. 5. cxd4 (or 5. Nf3 Nc6 6. cxd4) is usually met with ...d6, preparing to chip away at the pawn chain, or ...e6. Although not as aggressive for Black, it allows for a more solid structure going into the middle game. 

2...d6?! is occasionally played, where Black just allows White to take the full centre, as is 2...e6!? with the idea of 3...d5 and potentially transposing into a French defence, advance variation. 

 History 
The earliest recorded game in this opening is Wolf Popert versus Howard Staunton, 1841.Popert v Staunton, 1841. Chessgames.com Staunton played 2...e6 and the game transposed into an advance French. It is named after Semyon Alapin, who played it first in Vienna in 1898.Alapin v Maroczy, 1898. Chessgames.comAlapin v Schiffers, 1898. Chessgames.comAlapin v Tarrasch, 1898. Chessgames.com

One of its leading adherents in the 20th century was Evgeny Sveshnikov, who remarked that "I can confidently say that the move 2. c3 has fed me and my family for almost forty years."

Deep Blue employed the Alapin against Kasparov in games 1 and 3 of their 1996 match.Deep Blue v Kasparov, 1996. Chessgames.com[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1070876 Deep Blue v Kasparov, 1996. Chessgames.com

Today it is a popular anti-Sicilian employed at the highest levels, including by Magnus Carlsen.e.g. Carlsen v Gukesh, 2023. Chessgames.com A similar line is to play c3 on the third move, after 3. Nf3. By delaying c3, Black faces different choices depending on how they moved, e.g. 2. Nf3 d6 3. c3 and were Black to play ...d5, as they might against 2. c3, they have lost a tempo.

body:
[Diagram:
- FEN: 2rnbqkb/1r1pp1pp/ppp5/1n5p/8/2P5/1P6/PP1P1PPP
]

Sicilian, Alapin
This move continues development for Black. It puts pressure on the e pawn, and aims to protect the d5 square. This variation is marginally preferred to the 2...d5 response, and is statistically a better win-rate for Black (as per ChessBase.com). 

White’s Responses

3.e5 immediately pressures the Black knight, and is by far the most popular response. It also continues White’s assault on the centre, and aims to reinforce with d4.

3.d3 and 3.d4 are playable, but more passive. d3 aims to protect the e pawn, while d4 simply continues with White’s original plan of controlling the d4 square - the goal of the Alapin opening.

Theory table
.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6

 3 Sicilian, Alapin e5Nd5  d3Nc6 

 Nunn's Chess Openings. 1999. John Nunn (Editor), Graham Burgess, John Emms, Joe Gallagher. .
 Modern Chess Openings: MCO-14. 1999. Nick de Firmian, Walter Korn. .

body:
[Diagram:
- FEN: 2rnbqkb/1r1pp1pp/ppp5/1n5p/1P6/8/1P6/PP1P1PPP
]

Sicilian, Alapin

3. e5
White’s move attacks the knight, and continues to push the centre. It forces Black to move their piece twice in the opening development, and removes the threat of Ng4 placement later in the opening.

The main line of 3...Nd5 is rather forced, as 3...Ng8? is quite passive whilst 3...Ne4?? 4.d3! traps the knight.

The other moves of Ng4 or Nh5 lead to immediate capture by the queen.

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...d5
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation | ECO Code: B22]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. c3 > 2...d5 (Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. c3 d5]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Alapin Sicilian
]

 2...d5 
Black is threatening to take on e4. White's best option is to take first, with 3. exd5. 

After 3. exd5 the main line continues 3...Qxd5, the Barmen variation, and White doesn't have Nc3 to kick the queen away. After 4. d4, it is possible for Black to win a pawn and go into an endgame,4...cxd4 5. cxd4 Nc6 6. Nf3 Bg4 7. Nc3 Bxf3 8. gxf3 Qxd4 9. Qxd4 Nxd4 10. Nb5! however White has adequate compensation and better practical chances. A more common plan is to leave White with an isolated queen's pawn position and control d5 with ...e6 and ...Nf6.e.g. 4...Nc6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. Be2 cxd4 7. cxd4 e6 8. Nc3 Qa5 9. h3 Bh5 10. O-O Nf6. 

Black's other line is 3...Nf6, christened the anti-Alapin gambit, which is similar to the Tal gambit. White has the time to defend the d-pawn, but Black is eager to give some material for rapid development, e.g. 4. c4 e6 5. dxe6 Bxe6.

 Bad moves 

A quick round up of the White's other turn three options, which they should discard: 

White cannot play Nc3 to defend the pawn, as their c-pawn already occupies c3. 

3. e5!? allows Black to play ...Bf5 & ...e6, reaching an advance French-style position with the strict improvement that Black has been able to develop their queen's bishop outside of the pawn chain first. Black has equalised.

3. d3?! to defend e4 leaves the pawn on c3 out of place. If White avoids taking on d5, they allow Black easy development and plenty of space, e.g. 3...Nc6 4. Nd2 Nf6 5. Ngf3 e5 6. Be2 Be7 7. O-O O-O. Black could also consider playing d4 themselves: 3...d4 4. cxd4 cxd4 5. Qa4+ Nc6 6. Nf3.

3. d4? and Black is better after 3...dxe4 4. dxc5 Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1 Nf6.

Theory table

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5
			
		3
	
			Sicilian, Alapin
		exd5Qxd5
		
	
			
		e5Nc6
		
	

 References 

 Notes

[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. c3 d5 3. exd5]
body:
[Diagram:
- FEN: 8/1P4P1/P1P1PPPR/NBQKBN2/1prnbqkb/nrpp2pp/p7/4pP2
- Name: Sicilian, Alapin
]

 3. exd5 
The natural move; eliminating the tension in the center, while bringing Black's queen to a more vulnerable position. 

Although White cannot immediately attack the Queen because of the pawn on c3, in some lines the Queen can be pinned to a captured pawn on d4 (eg. 4. d4 cxd4 5. Nf3), or become a target later down the line with moves such as c4. However, the Black Queen on d5 is often one of Black's biggest assets, as it assists in ideas such as Bg4 and is exceedingly hard to kick out before White castles.  

3. exd5 is the most common move after 2...d5, followed by 3. d3 and 3. e5.

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit | ECO Code: B21]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. d4 (Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Sicilian defence
]

 2. d4 
White opens up the centre immediately. This is an uncommon but tactical sideline to avoid the conventional Open Sicilian. Today it is played with the idea of sacrificing a pawn for development and open lines.

Black should play 2...cxd4, which was why they played 1...c5 in the first place. 

In the 19th century, 2. d4 was played with the idea of opening the centre and recapturing the pawn immediately: 2...cxd4 3. Qxd4!?. This is sometimes seen today, but it allows Black to develop with tempo on the queen (3...Nc6) for an even game. White has to move their queen again and suddenly their development advantage, and the whole reason for opening the centre in the first place, disappears. 

3. Nf3, the Morphy gambit, sought to improve on 3. Qxd4 by preparing to retake with the knight. 3...Nc6 (say) 4. Nxd4 transposes back into the modern open Sicilian. However, Black has the addition resource of 3...e5!, securing the extra pawn and avoiding the transposition (4. Nxe5?? Qa5+!). 

Shuffling the move order gives us the modern main line: 2. Nf3 first, so that a. White can recapture on d4 with the knight not the queen, preserving tempo, and b. Black doesn't have time to play ...e5 and defend their d4 pawn. 

So is 2. d4 best consigned to the history books? No, because of the aggressive Smith-Morra gambit.

Rather than retake the pawn, White can gambit it with 3. c3, the Smith-Morra gambit. If Black accepts, 3...dxc4 4. Nxc3, Black gets to keep the pawn but White is ahead in development with an open centre and lots of attacking opportunities.

Anything other than 2...cxd4 for Black (2...d5?, 2...e6?!) is at best dubious. If Black wishes to avoid the Smith-Morra, then they're better off playing 2...cxd4 3. c3 d5 or 3...Nf6, transposing into an Alapin Sicilian.

title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4
moves_pgn: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit | ECO Code: B21]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. d4 > 2...cxd4 (Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Sicilian defence
]

2...cxd4 
Black takes the pawn. The trade of a c- for d-pawn gives Black a central pawn majority. 

Though White could take it back with 3. Qxd4?!, this allows Black to push the queen around and play 3...Nc6 with tempo. 

Instead the main move is 3. c3, the Smith-Morra gambit. After 3...dxc3 White can retake while developing their knight. 

An alternative is 3. Nf3, the Morphy gambit. White prepares to recapture with the knight. If Black tries to holds onto the extra pawn with 3...e5, White's best continuation is 4. c3 leading to something similar to the Smith-Morra, where Black has a hole on d5 and a backward d-pawn. Otherwise, this can transpose into an Open Sicilian after (e.g.) 3...d6 4. Nxd4. 

History
2. d4 was in vogue in the mid-19th century. Jaenisch, in his 1842 book of analysis, gave 2. d4 as White's best move against the Sicilian. 3. Qxd4 and 3. Nf3 were the continuations of the day; Jaenisch's gave preference to 2...cxd4 3. Qxd4, even though 3...Nc6 4. Qd1 allows Black to gain time on the queen. (translation of ) 

An early appearance of the gambit 3. c3 was in 1846 in Kieseritzky v Vitzthum.Kieseritzky v Vitzthum, 1846 - Chessgames.com It went largely un-played for the next century, aside from a few games in the 1920s and 1930s, until it was revived in the 1950s. Kenneth Smith (1930―1999) and Pierre Morra (1900―1969) independently published analysis of it in the 50s. Another proponent was Milan Matulović (1935―2013), after whom it was sometimes called (the Matulović gambit). 

Its leading proponent today is IM Marc Esserman (1983―).

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Morphy Gambit | ECO Code: B21]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. d4 > 2...cxd4 > 3. Nf3 (Sicilian Defense: Morphy Gambit)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. Nf3]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Morphy gambit
]

 3. Nf3 · Morphy gambit 

Rather than recapture the pawn with their queen, which would allow Black to gain tempo with ...Nc6, White prepares to recapture with their knight. 

This looks to transpose into a regular open Sicilian. Black may play whatever move they would have played after 2. Nf3 (3...d6, 3...Nc6 etc.) and allow the transposition.

However, the way to "punish" White for the irregular move order is 3...e5, securing the pawn. 4. Nxe5?? fails to 4...Qa5+!. White's best continuation is 4. c3, the Andreaschek gambit, reaching a position similar to the Smith-Morra gambit when declined with ...e5.  

 History 

This line was popular in the nineteenth century. One of its earliest appearances was von der Lasa versus Mayet, 1857.von der Lasa v. Mayet, 1857. Chessgames.com Paul Morphy played it frequently to reach open Sicilian positionsMorphy v Anderssen, 1858. Chessgames.comMorphy v Paulsen, 1857. Chessgames.com but also faced the line with 3...e5.Morphy v Journoud, 1858. Chessgames.comMorphy v Prett, 1858. Chessgames.com

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Sicilian defence
]

 3. Qxd4!? 

This move is not the best: though White regains the pawn, Black can harass White's queen with 3...Nc6. Black gets the initiative and nullifies White's first-turn advantage. 

However, 3. Qxd4!? Nc6 is not losing for White: at worst it is an even game, and the continuation 4. Qd3 has been occasionally explored as an anti-theory opening weapon.e.g. Chigaev vs Vakhidov, 2025. Chessgames.com

 History 
This line was first seen in the 1840s, when Sicilian defence theory was in its infancy. Howard Staunton explored this line against John Cochrane in a match series in 1842.Staunton v Cochrane, 1842. title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3
header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit | ECO Code: B21]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. d4 > 2...cxd4 > 3. c3 (Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit
]

 3. c3 · Smith-Morra gambit 
White offers a pawn for quicker development and open c- and d-files. 

3...dxc3 accepts the gambit, and White can recapture with 4. Nxc3. Black is now a pawn up, but in return White has a lead in development. They are ready to develop both their bishops, but Black will have to make two more pawn moves before they can get their bishops out. The game usually continues 4...Nc6 5. Nf3 e6 6. Bc4, where Black reaches the first major branching point in theory.   

Accepting is the main move, and the choice of chess engines (who are fearless). However, White gets good compensation for the pawn and attacking chances, so it is not uncommon to decline it. 

 Transpose into an Alapin Sicilian 

There are a few ways Black may decline the gambit and reach a position similar to the Alapin Sicilian (1. e4 c5 2. c3). 

3...Nf6 looks to transpose into the ...Nf6 line of the Alapin. The game continues 4. e5 Nd4 5. Nf3 Nc6 6. cxd4 and the same Alapin position is reached. This line is often preferred because because Black can answer the Alapin and Smith-Morra with the same preparation. 

3...d5, the Scandinavian variation, may transpose into the Barman line of the Alapin Sicilian (where 2. c3 is answered with 2...d5). A nuance is that in the Barman defence Black has the option to delay ...cxd4 to prevent White from opening the c3 square for their knight until after White has committed to Na3, but in the Smith-Morra move order Black has already played ...cxd4. 

 Other ways to decline 

3...d3, the push variation, offers the pawn back to White in a way that leaves White's c-pawn blocking their knight's preferred square. This avoids giving White extra tempi (White will have to move their c-pawn again to develop their knight). After 4. Bxd3 Nc6 5. c4, White has a strong control over d5. 

3...e5, the centre variation, allows White to recover the pawn and also get their knights out: 4. cxd4 exd4 5. Nf3 Nc6 6. Nxd4. 

3...Qa5!?, the wing variation, pins the c3-pawn. White can recover the material with 4. Nf3 Nc6 5. Nxd4, or they may first incorporate 5. b4! Qc7 6. b5, and 6...Ne5 7. Nxe5 Qxe5 8. Qxd4.

3...e5, the centre variation, allows White to recover the pawn and also get their knights out: 4. cxd4 exd4 5. Nf3 Nc6 6. Nxd4. 

3...Qa5!?, the wing variation, pins the c3-pawn. White can recover the material with 4. Nf3 Nc6 5. Nxd4, or they may first incorporate 5. b4! Qc7 6. b5, and 6...Ne5 7. Nxe5 Qxe5 8. Qxd4.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit accepted
]

 3...dxc4 · Smith-Morra gambit accepted 

Black accepts the gambit by taking another pawn. 

4. Nxc3 retakes the pawn while developing a piece. White's advantage is that they have managed to move both their e- and d-pawns, meaning they are ready to develop both their bishops without making any more pawn moves, without Black having had time to develop anything. All they had to give up was their central d-pawn: Black's advantage is that they are a pawn up and have both d- and e-pawns on the board.

Offering up another pawn, e.g. 4. Bc4? cxb2 5. Bxb2 à la the Danish gambit is considered to give up too much material for the compensation on offer, but it is aggressive and may still be played especially at shorter time controls. 

4. bxc3?? is inferior: preventing the development of the knight to c3, and leaving White with isolated a- and c-pawns, gives them no compensation for the sacrifice.

 4. Nxc3

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit accepted
]

 4...Nc6 
Black gets the development of their pieces underway and starts to control the centre and the d4 and e5 squares. Control of e5 prevents White pushing a pawn there, at least for now, and control of d4 means Black has the option of developing their king's bishop with ...e6 and ...Bb4 without allowing Qd4 to attack b4 and the g7-pawn.

5. Nf3 is White's main move, followed by 6. Bc4 to develop and to prepare to castle kingside. (White surely doesn't want to castle queenside into the open c-file open.)

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted | ECO Code: B21]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. d4 > 2...cxd4 > 3. c3 > 3...dxc3 > 4. Nxc3 > 4...Nc6 > 5. Nf3 (Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 Nc6 5. Nf3]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit accepted
]

 5. Nf3 
White continues development. They plan to follow up with 6. Bc4 and 7. O-O. 

Black usually wants to start thinking about a pawn move:

5...e6 is the main move. This opens a line for the king's bishop to develop. Since Black expects 6. Bc4, ...e6 has the added advantage of relieving the bishop's pressure on f7. After 6. Bc4, the game reaches the main tabiya of the Smith-Morra accepted, where Black's main choices are 6...a6, playing in the style of the Paulsen, 6...d6, playing in the style of the Scheveningen, 6...Qc7, the Siberian variation, or 6...Bb4, the pin variation.  

5...d6 is also played. After 6. Bc4, Black often wishes to play ...e6 as well, relieving the pressure on f7. (A common trap that fails to appreciate the danger of White's bishop is 5...d6 6. Bc4 Nf6 7. e5 Nxe5? 8. Nxe5 dxe5 9. Bxf7+! Kxf7 10. Qxd8 .) 

The two choices are to transpose into the Scheveningen line with 6...e6, where the plan is to eventually push ...e5 to free the queen's bishop (7. O-O Be7 8. Qe2 Nf6 9. Rd1 e5 ), or the classical line, which plays ...e6 only after Black has traded off the queen's bishop to prevent the bishop from being stuck behind the e-pawn (6...a6 7. O-O Nf6 8. Bf4 Bg4 9. h3 Bxf3 10. Qxf3 e6 ). 

5...g6, the fianchetto defence, is a small sideline. This prepares ...Bg7. A drawback is that Black does not want to combine ...g6 and ...e6 because of how it will weaken Black's dark squares around their king. (6. Bc4 Bg7 7. O-O e6? 8. Nb5!  and the threats of Qd6 and Bf4 are deadly.)  

It is also possible to play 5...Nf6 first, as although White's knight now allows them to play 6. e5 to kick the knight, it also allows Black's knight to hop to 6...Ng4. Usually it is just a move order difference and after 6. Bc4, Black commits to a pawn move anyway.

header:
[Opening: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted | ECO Code: B21]
[Path: Chess Opening Theory > 1. e4 > 1...c5 > 2. d4 > 2...cxd4 > 3. c3 > 3...dxc3 > 4. Nxc3 > 4...Nc6 > 5. Nf3 > 5...d6 > 6. Bc4 (Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted)]
[PGN Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 Nc6 5. Nf3 d6 6. Bc4]
body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit accepted
]

 6. Bc4 

White's bishop pressures Black's vulnerable f7 pawn. The strength of the bishop's pressure can be seen in a number of traps Black can fall into with imprecise play. Black can blunt its attack by pushing the pawn ...e6, though the question is, now or later? 

6...e6 is the most straight forward and main move. This reaches a Scheveningen-style structure, otherwise reached after the line 5...e6 6. Bc4 d6. This only requires a small amount of patience: Black is preparing to play ...e5 and to allow the bishop back into the game. The line continues 7. O-O Nf6 8. Qe2 Be7 9. Rd1 e5 10. Be3 O-O 11. Rac1. 

Playing ...e5 in two moves (6...e6 then 9...e5) looks like a waste of tempo, but it is necessary for Black to manage the pressure on f7. 6...e5? allows 7. Ng5! for an attack on f7. 7...Nh6 8. Qf3 f6 is forced, but this allows 9. Ne6! Bxe6 10. Bxe6 . Black may think they have Nd4 with tempo and Nc2+, however Black can quickly become undone. 10...Nd4 11. Qh3 and White threatens Bxh6!! (the bishop cannot be recaptured because of Qh5+ and Qf7#!). 11...Nc2+ 12. Kf1 does nothing about the threat of Bxh6. 11. Nxe6? 12. Qxe6 Qe7 13. Qc4 and White threatens Nd4, Bxh6, and Black's position is tied up in knots.

But by first playing ...e6, the bishop's pressure on f7 is nullified while Black plays ...Be7, ...Nf6 and ...O-O. Then, with their rook guarding f7, it is safe enough for Black to push ...e5. In this way, ...e6 is necessary preparation for ...e5. 

Since Black played 5...d6 to open a diagonal for their bishop, they may dislike the idea of spending another tempo to block it immediately. Is there a way to develop the bishop outside the pawn chain first? 

Yes, but not immediately. First it must be prepared by 6...a6. Why?

6...Bg4? runs into the classic trap where White sacrifices their bishop to draw the king into range of the pinned knight. 7. Bxf7+! Kxf7 8. Ng5+ Ke8 9. Qxg4 . Therefore Black must ensure the bishop will be defended on g4, by first controlling the square with ...Nf6. 

However, Black can't play 6...Nf6 and 7...Bg5 straight away either, again due to the pressure White exerts on f7. 7. e5! and: 

 7...Nxe5?? 8. Nxe5 and the threat is Bxf7#. 
 8...dxe5?? allows 9. Bxf7+! Kxf7 10. Qxd8. 
 8...e6 9. Bb5+, and after trading off the minor pieces, 9...Nd7 10. Bxd7+ Bxd7 11. Nxd7 Qxd7, 12. Qd4! . Black is down material and never getting to develop. 
 7...dxe5?! 8. Qxd8+ and either way to retake the queen leads to issues.
 8...Kxd8 9. Ng5 threatens Nxf7+. 9...Na5 to attack the bishop is most resourceful, then 10. Bb5 Be6 (to deal with the threat of Nxf7+) 11. Nxe6+ fxe6, Black's left with triple isolated pawns  
 8...Nxd8 9. Nb5! threatens Nc7+. The king can't move (9...Kd7?? 10. Nxe5+ Ke8 11. Nc7#) so the rook must, 9...Rb8, then 10. Nxe5 and 10...e6 is force to prevent Nc7#. 

The only way for Black to hold the position is 7...Ng4 8. exd6 exd6, and it looks like the bishop isn't getting to g4 anyway. (9. O-O Bf5? instead and there's a flashy sequence 10. Re1 Be7 11. Bxf7! Kxf7 Qd5+!)

So in order to play ...Bg4, Black needs to play ...Nf6, and in order to play ...Nf6 they need to prepare it with 6...a6. This controls the b5 square, which means that after 7. O-O Nf6, reaching a classical Sicilian structure, the line 8. e5? dxe5 9. Qxd6 Nxd8 goes nowhere for White, because they don't have the resource of Nb5. The game continues 8. Bf4 Bg4 9. h3 Bxf3 10. Qxf3, where Black, having dispensed with the bad bishop, can now happily play 10...e6.

(the bishop cannot be recaptured because of Qh5+ and Qf7#!). 11...Nc2+ 12. Kf1 does nothing about the threat of Bxh6. 11. Nxe6? 12. Qxe6 Qe7 13. Qc4 and White threatens Nd4, Bxh6, and Black's position is tied up in knots.

But by first playing ...e6, the bishop's pressure on f7 is nullified while Black plays ...Be7, ...Nf6 and ...O-O. Then, with their rook guarding f7, it is safe enough for Black to push ...e5. In this way, ...e6 is necessary preparation for ...e5. 

Since Black played 5...d6 to open a diagonal for their bishop, they may dislike the idea of spending another tempo to block it immediately. Is there a way to develop the bishop outside the pawn chain first? 

Yes, but not immediately. First it must be prepared by 6...a6. Why?

6...Bg4? runs into the classic trap where White sacrifices their bishop to draw the king into range of the pinned knight. 7. Bxf7+! Kxf7 8. Ng5+ Ke8 9. Qxg4 . Therefore Black must ensure the bishop will be defended on g4, by first controlling the square with ...Nf6. 

However, Black can't play 6...Nf6 and 7...Bg5 straight away either, again due to the pressure White exerts on f7. 7. e5! and: 

 7...Nxe5?? 8. Nxe5 and the threat is Bxf7#. 
 8...dxe5?? allows 9. Bxf7+! Kxf7 10. Qxd8. 
 8...e6 9. Bb5+, and after trading off the minor pieces, 9...Nd7 10. Bxd7+ Bxd7 11. Nxd7 Qxd7, 12. Qd4! . Black is down material and never getting to develop. 
 7...dxe5?! 8. Qxd8+ and either way to retake the queen leads to issues.
 8...Kxd8 9. Ng5 threatens Nxf7+. 9...Na5 to attack the bishop is most resourceful, then 10. Bb5 Be6 (to deal with the threat of Nxf7+) 11. Nxe6+ fxe6, Black's left with triple isolated pawns  
 8...Nxd8 9. Nb5! threatens Nc7+. The king can't move (9...Kd7?? 10. Nxe5+ Ke8 11. Nc7#) so the rook must, 9...Rb8, then 10. Nxe5 and 10...e6 is force to prevent Nc7#. 

The only way for Black to hold the position is 7...Ng4 8. exd6 exd6, and it looks like the bishop isn't getting to g4 anyway. (9. O-O Bf5? instead and there's a flashy sequence 10. Re1 Be7 11. Bxf7! Kxf7 Qd5+!)

So in order to play ...Bg4, Black needs to play ...Nf6, and in order to play ...Nf6 they need to prepare it with 6...a6. This controls the b5 square, which means that after 7. O-O Nf6, reaching a classical Sicilian structure, the line 8. e5? dxe5 9. Qxd6 Nxd8 goes nowhere for White, because they don't have the resource of Nb5. The game continues 8. Bf4 Bg4 9. h3 Bxf3 10. Qxf3, where Black, having dispensed with the bad bishop, can now happily play 10...e6.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit accepted
]

 5...e6 
Black has opened a line for the king's bishop to develop, and the pawn on e6 has the added advantage of relieving the bishop's pressure on f7. 

Nevertheless, 6. Bc4 is the main move. White still would like to develop their king's bishop and prepare to castle, and c4 is as good a square as any. The game reaches the main tabiya of the Smith-Morra accepted and Black chooses between 6...a6, playing in the style of the Paulsen, 6...d6, playing in the style of the Scheveningen, 6...Qc7, the Siberian variation, or 6...Bb4, the pin variation.  

6. Be2 is reasonable alternative but uncommon; it at least allows White to castle. 

6. Bb5?! gives Black fuel to start expanding on the queen's side with 6...a6 7. Ba4 (7. Bxc6? bxc6. White has already given up a pawn and is doing Black's job for them if they also start trading down) b5, and the bishop ends up on the same restricted diagonal as if White had played 6. Bc4.

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Fianchetto defence
]

 5...g6 · Fianchetto defence 
Black prepares to fianchetto their bishop, playing in the style of the accelerated dragon Sicilian. This is a playable but sharp line, and Black needs to be accurate to hold the position.  

6. Bc4 develops the bishop, prepares to castle, and places pressure on f7. 6...Bg7 and White has the interesting move 7. e5. The e-pawn is not in fact hanging because of tactics emerging from White's bishop (7...Nxe5?! 8. Nxe5 Bxe5 9. Bxf7+ Kxf7 10. Qd5+ Kg7 11. Qxe5+ Nf6 ). While it is on e5, it prevents Black's knight from developing to f6, and if Black removes it with 7...d6 8. exd6 they may not recapture the pawn yet because of 8...exd6? 9. Nb5!. 

One difficulty Black faces in the 5...g6 move order is how best to address White's latent pressure on f7. In other lines like 5...d6 6. Bc4, Black can play 6...e6, however the combination of ...g6 an ...e6 is dangerous because of how much it weakens the dark squares around Black's king. For instance, 6...Bg7 7. O-O e6? 8. Nb5! Nf6 9. Qd6! (see diagram) and White is threatening Nc7+. 

[Diagram:
- Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 Nc6 5. Nf3 g6 6. Bc4 Bg7 7. O-O e6 8. Nb5 Nf6 9. Qd6
- Name: After 9. Qd6!, possible because both the e6 pawn and Black's king's bishop have left d6 undefended, White threatens Nc7+. Black's best continuation is 9...Qe7 10. Nc7+ Kd8 11. Qxe7+ Kxe7 12. Nxa8 .
]

body:
[Diagram:
- Name: Smith-Morra gambit accepted
]

 4. bxc3?? 

White forgets why they offered the pawn sacrifice 3. c3 in the first place. Slavish adherence to the rule of "capture towards the centre" has lead them here, down a pawn, with isolated a- and c-pawns, nothing developed, and with their knight unable to reach c3. 

Black should have an easy game.

 Sicilian Defense: Pawn Push Variation 
This rarely seen move has some logical basis. The pawn on e5 prevents Black playing Nf6 and so the Black Kingside is cramped for a while. White can support the e5 pawn with Nf3. The drawback for White of 2.e5 is no added pressure is brought to the center, especially on d4 or d5 and the extra tempo allows Black various options, the main one is play Nc6 which hinders White's d4 move as well as attacking the as yet undefended e5 pawn.

body:
[Diagram:
- FEN: 2rnbqkb/nr1pp1pp/ppp5/7p/8/2PP4/8/PPPP2PP
]

 2. f4 · McDonnell attack 

With 2. f4 White begins an aggressive attack against Black's kingside. This is the McDonnell attack, aka  a(n accelerated) Grand Prix. 

2...d5, the Tal gambit, lets Black thwart the attack before it gets started. If White declines with 3. e5, Black can play Bf5 and e6, achieving a superior French defence structure without the lousy French bishop. If White accepts, 3. exd5, Black can recover the pawn and get a development lead: 3...Nf6 4. Nc3 Nxd5 5. Nxd5 Qxd5.  

For this reason the attack is often played in the move order 2. Nc3 followed by 3. f4, the (conventional) Grand Prix, where if e.g. 2. Nc3 Nc6 3. f4 e5 can be met with Nxe5. 

Quieter second moves for Black, continuing however they would against an Open or Closed Sicilian--2...Nc6, 2...e6, so on--are also very playable, but don't capitalise on the position as much as the Tal Gambit. 

 History 

2. f4 was played many times by Alexander McDonnell as White against La Bourdonnais in their 1834 match series. La Bourdonnais was considered the strongest player of his generation, and their confrontation a precursor to the modern world chess championship. His success with the Sicilian defence in these matches was later credited with reviving the interest in the opening.
